title: Beijing and Berlin Used the Same Word: "Campaign"
subtitle: US sanctions on the ICC's Japanese president produced cross-bloc consensus with no visible defender
body_md:
China's state broadcaster and Germany's public broadcaster agree on very little. On August 18, they used the same word.

[CGTN World](https://news.cgtn.com/news/2026-08-19/US-sanctions-ICC-president-senior-lawyer-1PJgicTfYT6/p.html?UTM_Source=cgtn&UTM_Medium=rss&UTM_Campaign=World) reported that Washington had stepped up its "campaign" against the International Criminal Court. [Deutsche Welle English](https://www.dw.com/en/us-imposes-new-sanctions-on-icc-president-senior-lawyer-in-latest-escalation/a-78420261?maca=en-rss-en-all-1573-rdf) headlined the move as the US announcing "additional sanctions on members of the ICC" in a story labeled "latest escalation." The word choice was not coordinated. It reflects a shared factual read: the US government sanctioned the ICC's president — Tomoko Akane of Japan — and a senior trial lawyer, Abdoulaye Seye of Senegal, adding both to the Treasury's Specially Designated Nationals list.

Eighteen outlets across thirteen countries covered the sanctions. None produced a credible defense of the US position. Secretary of State Rubio provided the formal rationale — the sanctioned individuals had "directly engaged in efforts by the ICC to investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute officials whose government has not consented to ICC jurisdiction," as [The Hindu Intl](https://www.thehindu.com/news/international/us-sanctions-icc-chief-tomoko-akane-of-japan/article71363112.ece) reported — but that framing received no uptake. [AFP / France 24 EN](https://www.france24.com/en/americas/20260818-icc-says-us-sanctions-on-top-court-members-undermine-rule-of-law) led its coverage with the ICC's own response: the measures "undermine the rule of law." That phrase echoed through wire services, Asian broadcasters, and European public media.

The convergence between Beijing and Berlin is the defining fact of this corpus. CGTN and DW approach US foreign policy from opposite institutional frameworks: one from a country outside the ICC that is broadly skeptical of Western-led legal architecture, one from a US treaty ally and ICC state party. The sanctions produced no ideological fault line that might otherwise organize press responses. Neither geopolitical alignment with Washington nor traditional opposition to it generated a voice willing to defend the action.

Three outlets supplied the dimensions absent from this consensus. [Japan Times](https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2026/08/19/world/politics/icc-us-sanctions-multilateralism/) alone framed the sanctions as a bilateral alliance dilemma: "The move by the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump presents a dilemma for Tokyo, a strong backer of multilateral groupings and a key American ally." Japan is a treaty ally whose own national now leads a court Washington is actively pressuring. That specific structural problem — the one most directly felt by a government with direct stakes — received almost no coverage outside Japan itself.

[Standard Kenya World](https://www.standardmedia.co.ke/world/article/2001555098/us-rights-groups-sue-trump-over-icc-sanctions) and [AllAfrica](https://allafrica.com/stories/202608190091.html) added a dimension entirely absent from Asian and European coverage: rights groups had filed suit against Trump in US federal court, arguing the sanctions "block victims of war crimes from pursuing justice." The conflict between US sanctions law and ICC access for war crime survivors is a distinct legal story from the geopolitical framing that dominates the rest of the corpus, and it was surfaced only by African-facing outlets — a significant editorial gap given the ICC's case docket, which includes numerous African situations.

[Anadolu Agency English](https://www.aa.com.tr/en/asia-pacific/tokyo-calls-us-sanctions-on-japanese-chief-of-icc-extremely-regrettable/4031268) was the only outlet to establish explicitly the causal chain most others omit: the current sanctions trace to the ICC's November 2024 arrest warrants for Netanyahu and Gallant. Without that context, the sanctions appear to be an institutional grievance rooted in abstract sovereignty objections. With it, they are a specific response to specific proceedings, and the pattern of escalation — each tranche of sanctions following a specific ICC action — becomes legible.

[NL Times](https://nltimes.nl/2026/08/19/us-sanctions-icc-chairman-prosecutor-latest-attack-court-hague) described the sanctions as "the latest attack on court in The Hague," grounding an abstract institutional story in a geographic one: the ICC sits in the Netherlands, and a host nation that cannot protect its court's officers from foreign sanctions is in an unusual position.

The silence the corpus cannot fill is Israeli. No Israeli outlet appeared in this cluster despite the Netanyahu arrest warrants being the stated trigger for the US pressure campaign. How Israeli press and government are framing the sanctions — as adequate protection, as embarrassing overreach, as insufficient — is entirely absent from eighteen-country coverage of an event that is, at its origin, about Israeli leaders.
